title: Lala's early trumpet bands and $125 a week
summary: Lala talks about leading bands in the city, paying $125 a week, the trumpet players he had (the Primas, cousin Mike Lala) and relieving the piano player.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: You know who the first band put a saxophone player in the jealous band in the city of
Oakland No. When I was playing, I had a band up there. I was getting 125 a week. I was playing trumpet.
And you played the piano? I played the waltzes. I played the waltzes. These were bands, you know?
Did you know Mario Filazzo? Yeah. A bass player? Yeah.

Well, he was good. He was good. He was an all-around man. Then you had Luba Prima. I had Luba Prima, Leon Prima. He was a legitimate. I had Luba Prima, Leon Prima, my little cousin Mike Lala. I had Tony this. I had more trumpet players.
Which Mike Lala are you talking about? The one they call Black Mike? Black Mike's my son. White Mike is your son? Yeah. My son, yeah. He plays a lot of trumpet.

And I had them all. I never touched a trumpet for two weeks. They always come up. Little Luba Prima, Leon Prima, a little Femulara. He was working in the theater. He'd come up there and play after. All I had, they made a carnet player line up by the minimums up there.
Even in those days, they had to go jam. They all had to come over with my beat and get jamming.
That's me. I was collecting the money, $125 a week. One thing I was doing, relieve the piano player. I never said to my trumpet for two weeks. Oh, okay. I was making one for the hour of the world.
That used to have a whole family bandstand. You had to call it the piano to get to it. Where was that? Fionn T used to be a perfect bandstand. Fionn T used to be a perfect bandstand.
